## Context

There are several components in Primer React that make use of live regions.
However, the library does not have a central pattern for making accessible live
region announcements. This ADR documents the decision to use a central pattern
for live region announcements that can be used across Primer and GitHub.

ARIA Live regions fall into several buckets that we may want to use as component
authors:

- [ARIA live region roles](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#live_region_roles), such as `alert`, `log`, or `status`
- [The `aria-live` attribute](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#aria-live) to turn an element into a live region

In components, we see the following scenarios in Primer React:

- Announce the contents of an element when it is rendered or on page load, like when a spinner is displayed or a form is submitted
- Announce the changes to the content of an element, like when the count inside of a
  button is incremented
- Announce a message programmatically, such as the number of results for a query

Currently, contributors may reach for roles such as `alert` or `status` to
achieve these scenarios. They may also add `aria-live="assertive"` or `aria-live="polite"` with an an `aria-atomic="true"` to an element explicitly.
However, both of these approaches do not announce consistently across screen
readers. This could be due to live regions being injected dynamically into the document (this includes loading content into the document via React), dynamically changing the visibility of a live region, or some other technique causing an announcement to not be announced.

For more information about the ways in which live regions may not work as
expected, visit: [Why are my live regions not working?](https://tetralogical.com/blog/2024/05/01/why-are-my-live-regions-not-working/)

## Decision

In order to have a common interop point for live region announcements, Primer React will
make use of a `live-region` custom element from `@primer/live-region-element`.
This package will be included and published from the `primer/react` repo.

The custom element exposes a way to make announcements that can be used
across frameworks. This makes it useful not only for Primer but GitHub as a
whole. The `@primer/live-region-element` exports two helpers to use for making
announcements: `announce()` and `announceFromElement`. Both helpers can be used
when working in Primer and by teams at GitHub.

In addition, `@primer/react` will leverage and export the following helpers for
use within Primer React and GitHub:

- The `AriaStatus` component to correspond with `role="status"`
- The `AriaAlert` component to correspond with `role="alert"`

Within `@primer/react`, we should lint against usage of `aria-live` and the
corresponding roles (if possible) and suggest using these alternatives instead.

> [!NOTE]
> Both `AriaStatus` and `AriaAlert` will trigger an announcement when the component is
> rendered. As a result, they should only be used for dynamically rendered
> content. Otherwise, they will trigger announcements on page load. In cases
> where they should always be present, then the first message passed to the
> component should be an empty string. Changes to the content of the component
> will trigger subsequent announcements.

## Context

> tl;dr
>
> We have workspaces within the project but no official way of connecting them or managing dependencies from the top-level. Similarly, scripts that grow in size or complexity have no dedicated home or ability to manage dependencies outside of the top-level workspace.

The `primer/react` repo is composed of several workspaces that use `npm` to manage dependencies. In order to install these dependencies, a contributor needs to visit each directory and run `npm install`. The project also has a convenience script for this task, invoked through `npm run setup`, that goes through this process for contributors.

These distinct workspaces may sometimes depend on each other. For example, the `docs` workspace depends on the `@primer/react` package which is defined at the top-level of the project. Similarly, examples in the `examples/*` folders may also depend on `@primer/react`. Currently these dependencies are expressed either through relative paths, file dependencies in `package.json`, or symlinks through `npm link`.

There is also a collection of scripts under the `script` directory that exist in the project that involve varying levels of complexity and depth.
decision:
## Decision 

We will adopt `turborepo` as the designated tool for managing JavaScript projects and workspaces within the `primer/react` repository.

**Core Benefits:**

*   **Improved Dependency Management:** `turborepo` will standardize how inter-workspace dependencies are declared and resolved, replacing the current ad-hoc methods (relative paths, `file:` dependencies, `npm link`). This will lead to a more robust and predictable dependency graph.
*   **Centralized Script Execution:** `turborepo`'s task runner will allow for a single command to execute scripts across multiple workspaces, simplifying common development tasks like `build`, `test`, or `lint`.
*   **Performance Optimization:** `turborepo`'s caching and parallel execution features will significantly speed up common development workflows, especially for tasks that span multiple workspaces.
*   **Simplified Setup:** The initial setup process for new contributors will be streamlined, reducing the need to manually `npm install` in each workspace.
*   **Scalability:** As the project grows and more workspaces or complex scripts are introduced, `turborepo` will provide a scalable and maintainable solution for managing them.

**Implementation Details:**

1.  **Installation:** `turborepo` will be installed as a dev dependency at the top-level of the `primer/react` repository.
2.  **Configuration:** A `turbo.json` file will be created at the top-level to define tasks, dependencies between tasks, and caching strategies.
3.  **Workspace Definition:** Existing `package.json` `workspaces` configurations will be leveraged by `turborepo`.
4.  **Script Migration:** Existing scripts, especially those in the `script` directory and `package.json` `scripts` sections, will be migrated to `turborepo` tasks where appropriate.
5.  **Documentation:** The project's contributing guidelines will be updated to reflect the use of `turborepo` for project setup and task execution.

## Context

Reasons for change: Performance, utilise css variables

The main reason for changing our styling architecture is to remove performance issues for applications:

Relevant parts from [primer/discussions#1928](https://github.com/github/primer/discussions/1928#reasons)(Hubbers only link):

1. Initial page loads take longer

   Because styles are injected during runtime, we can not parallelize this work. The page is un-styled till the javascript bundle is
   downloaded and processed. The processing time is longer on slower devices.

   Benchmarks:

   i. Lab benchmarks: rendering a page with 1000 components
   runtime injection of css: 242ms
   static .css files: 96ms (60% faster)

   ii. Application benchmarks: render times for repo directory (>1000 files, [gh/gh#241090](https://github.com/github/github/pull/241090))
   with primer/react Box: 3800ms
   with custom css: 3076ms (20% faster)

2. Slow server side rendering

   Some applications are able to make up for slower initial render times by collecting styles on the server first. In the correct stack, collecting styles requires rendering the app twice before we can ship any html to the user.

   benchmarks: in the issues-app experiment, collecting styles on the server contributed to + 20% of rendering time (450ms on top of 1900ms)

3. Style updates are expensive

   The slowest part of the current stack is updating styles based on props or state. Big changes take linearly longer, worse on slower devices.

   Benchmarks:

   i. Lab benchmarks: updating a page with 1000 components, static runtime css vs. dynamic runtime css (thanks @mattcosta7 for these!)

   re-rendering components with fixed styles on runtime: 242ms
   re-rendering components with dynamic styles on runtime: 441ms (55% slower)

   ii. Application benchmarks: opting out of IconButton for PR diff view (>500 files, [gh/gh#243269](https://github.com/github/github/pull/243269))

   dynamic styles with sx prop: 400ms
   dynamic styles with .css files: 165ms (60% faster)

The other reasons for change are to utilise css variables for theming and improve the guardrails of consuming primer/primitives
decision:
## Decision
We are changing our styling architecture from `@primer/react`’s `sx` prop to a new approach that extracts styles to static CSS files for production and uses CSS variables for theming. This will result in better performance, better guarding primitives, and a simpler mental model for developers.

**Detailed changes:**

1.  **Component Styling:**
    *   **From:** `sx` prop, which uses Emotion to generate and inject styles at runtime.
    *   **To:** A new system where component styles are extracted into static `.css` files during the build process. These `.css` files will be served and loaded by the browser directly.
    *   **Impact:** Eliminates runtime style injection overhead, enabling parallelization of style loading and faster initial page loads. Reduces the cost of style updates and improves server-side rendering performance.

2.  **Theming:**
    *   **From:** Theme values and styling logic managed by Emotion within JavaScript.
    *   **To:** CSS variables will be the primary mechanism for theming. Primitives values (colors, spacing, typography) will be exposed as CSS custom properties.
    *   **Impact:** Leverages native browser capabilities for dynamic styling, improves performance, and simplifies theme management.

3.  **Guardrails for Primitives:**
    *   **From:** Less strict enforcement of design token usage, allowing for direct CSS values via `sx`.
    *   **To:** The new architecture will inherently provide stronger guardrails, encouraging the use of predefined CSS variables (which are driven by Primer Primitives) rather than arbitrary values. This will be enforced through tooling or conventions.
    *   **Impact:** Ensures design consistency, reduces the likelihood of custom one-off styles, and reinforces the use of the design system.

4.  **Developer Experience:**
    *   **From:** React component-centric styling with a mix of inline styles and Emotion's CSS-in-JS.
    *   **To:** A more traditional CSS-based approach for production, with a focus on pre-compiled styles. The exact developer interface (e.g., how developers define styles that get extracted) will be part of the implementation details but will aim to be intuitive and efficient.
    *   **Impact:** Simplifies the mental model by separating presentation from logic at runtime, potentially easing debugging and performance optimization efforts.

This decision addresses the identified performance bottlenecks and aligns with the goal of better leveraging native browser capabilities for styling and theming.

## Context

There are situations where a component prop can support a value or a "responsive
value" that results in the value changing depending on the viewport size. For
example:

```tsx
// Value
<Stack gap="condensed" />

// Responsive value
<Stack gap={{ narrow: 'condensed', regular: 'normal', wide: 'spacious' />
```

Typically, a responsive value will support all of our named breakpoints: narrow,
regular, and wide. Authors can use a hook called `useResponsiveValue` to support
resolving the value of a prop based on the current viewport size. The
implementation of this hook uses [`matchMedia`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/matchMedia)
which, unfortunately, has a downside: the value of a prop may shift when the
component is server-side rendered. If the prop is used for styles or layout, then this will lead to a layout shift
when the component hydrates and the viewport size is different than the fallback
size on the server.

As a result, we would like to offer a paved path for providing responsive props
in a way tha twill not lead to layout shift during server-side rendering.

## Context

There are times when a prop is deprecated in favor of a more accessible API or a more flexible prop that can support a wider range of values. In these cases, we want to provide a clear path for authors to migrate from the deprecated prop to the new API.

For

```tsx

<ActionList>
  <ActionList.Group title="Group title">
    <ActionList.Item>Item 1</ActionList.Item>
    <ActionList.Item>Item 2</ActionList.Item>
  </ActionList.Group>
</ActionList>
```

```tsx

<ActionList>
  <ActionList.Group>
    <ActionList.GroupHeading as="h2">Group title</ActionList.GroupHeading>
    <ActionList.Item>Item 1</ActionList.Item>
    <ActionList.Item>Item 2</ActionList.Item>
  </ActionList.Group>
</ActionList>
```

  - http://proxy.com
  - http://127.0.0.1:8080
  - http://user:password@proxy.com

  - http://127.0.0.1:8080
  - http://user:password@proxy.com

Command echoing as a default behavior tends to clutter the user logs, so we want to swap to a system where users have to opt in to see this information.

Command outputs will still be echoed in the case there are any errors processing such commands. This is so the end user can have more context on why the command failed and help with troubleshooting.

## Context

This ADR proposes adding `steps.<id>.outcome` and `steps.<id>.conclusion` to the steps context.

This allows downstream a step to run based on whether a previous step succeeded or failed.

Reminder, currently the steps contains `steps.<id>.outputs`.
decision:
## Decision 
We will add `steps.<id>.outcome` and `steps.<id>.conclusion` to the `steps` context.

**`steps.<id>.outcome`** will be set to the result of a completed step after it has completed. It will be one of `success`, `failure`, `cancelled`, or `skipped`.

**`steps.<id>.conclusion`** will be set to the final conclusion of a completed step after it has completed. It will be one of `success`, `failure`, `cancelled`, or `skipped`.

The `outcome` can be set to `failure` but the `conclusion` can still be `success` if `continue-on-error` is set to `true`.

The `conclusion` can be set to `skipped` if an `if` condition on the step itself evaluates to `false`.

For example, a step that runs a script:

```yaml
- name: Run a script
  id: my-script
  run: echo "Hello world!"
```

The output of `steps.my-script.outcome` will be `success` if the script exits with a zero exit code, and `failure` if the script exits with a non-zero exit code.
The output of `steps.my-script.conclusion` will be `success` if `continue-on-error` is set to `true` and the script exits with a non-zero exit code.

This allows a subsequent step to determine whether a previous step succeeded or failed, regardless of whether `continue-on-error` was set.

## Context
SS?? fundamentally relies on a third-party provider service to authenticate requests (e.g. OAuth2
via Google). The provider may experience transient faults for any number of reasons - perhaps the
provider is experiencing a transient outage, or our traffic has been temporarily rate limited. We
wanted to build SS?? to anticipate and handle the presence of faults during communication with
authentication providers, no matter the underlying cause.
decision:
## Decision
The decision made was to implement and configure a circuit breaker pattern within the authentication
flow. A circuit breaker is a design pattern used in software development to detect failures and
encapsulate the logic of preventing a fault from constantly recurring. The main idea of a circuit
breaker is that when a system experiences a high rate of failures, it "breaks" the circuit and
stops sending requests to the failing system, thereby preventing it from being overwhelmed.

Specifically, we decided on the following:

- **Library Choice**: We chose to integrate a battle-tested circuit breaker library into our authentication service. (The specific library name isn't mentioned in the context, but would typically be included in a real ADR).
- **Configuration**:
    - **Failure Threshold**: The circuit breaker will be configured to "trip" (open) if a certain percentage of authentication requests to the third-party provider fail within a defined time window.
    - **Timeout**: Each individual request to the authentication provider will have a timeout. If a request exceeds this timeout, it will be considered a failure.
    - **Open State Duration**: Once the circuit breaker is open, it will remain in this state for a configurable duration. During this time, all authentication requests will immediately fail without attempting to contact the provider.
    - **Half-Open State**: After the open state duration, the circuit breaker will transition to a "half-open" state. In this state, a limited number of "test" requests will be allowed through to the authentication provider.
    - **Reset/Reopen**: If these test requests succeed, the circuit breaker will close, and normal operation will resume. If they fail, the circuit breaker will return to the open state for another duration.
- **Fallback Mechanism**: When the circuit breaker is open or half-open and requests are failing, a fallback mechanism will be implemented. This will typically involve:
    - Returning an appropriate error message to the client indicating a temporary authentication issue.
    - Potentially redirecting to a cached authentication state if available and valid (though the context doesn't explicitly state this, it's a common pattern with circuit breakers).
    - Logging the circuit breaker state changes and failed attempts for monitoring and debugging.

This implementation allows SS?? to gracefully degrade in the event of upstream authentication provider issues, protecting both the provider from further load during a fault and the SS?? service from becoming unresponsive due to repeated failed calls.
predicted_decision:
## Decision
We implemented a generic `circuit.Breaker` type, which implements the "Circuit Breaker" design
pattern made popular by Michael T. Nygard's book, ["Release It!"](
https://pragprog.com/book/mnee/release-it). All requests to the provider service are issued through
a stateful `circuit.Breaker` instance, which tracks the frequency of request failures. When the
`Breaker` sees that enough requests are failing, it temporarily suspends all outgoing traffic to the
provider (i.e. "enters `Open` state). After some time, the `Breaker` transitions to a `HalfOpen`
state, in which a limited number of outbound requests are allowed. If failures persist, then the
`Breaker` will once again suspend outbound traffic, re-enter `Open` state, and typically will wait
for a longer interval of time before trying again. If instead the `Breaker` observes that requests
are consistently succeeding, then it will resume all outbound traffic (i.e. enter `Closed` state).

The SS?? [`docs`](/docs/) directory contains a [Circuit Breaker](
/docs/architecture/circuit-breaker.md) document with more details. The implementation can be found
in [`breaker.go`](/internal/auth/circuit/breaker.go)

## Context

Extensions are defined by an EDN file accessed from decentralized storage. An URI schema allows to identify those files.
decision:
## Decision 
### Identified problem
The current URI schema to identify extensions has a few drawbacks:
- it forces the use of a hash
- it does not allow for identifying extensions from IPNS

### Options considered
1. Adding a new URI schema
2. Extending the current URI schema

#### Option 1 (adding a new URI schema)
A new URI schema (e.g., `ipns://`) could be added to support IPNS-identified extensions. This new schema would be processed distinctly from the `ipfs://` schema.
A similar approach would be to specify the identification method in the current URI schema, e.g., `ipfs://hash?method=ipns`.

This option has a few benefits:
- it clearly separates the two methods of identification
- it's easy to implement

However, it also has some drawbacks:
- it means that two different URIs can point to the same file

#### Option 2 (extending the current URI schema)
The current URI schema could be extended by allowing to provide a hash as well as an IPNS name. If both are provided, the hash takes precedence.
For example, the following URIs would be valid:
- `ipfs://hash`
- `ipfs://ipns-name`
- `ipfs://hash?name=ipns-name`

This option has a few benefits:
- it makes the hash optional
- it clearly indicates that `ipns-name` identifies an IPNS record
- it allows for providing both the hash and the IPNS name, which is useful for caching purposes

However, it also has some drawbacks:
- it's not as clear as the previous option

### Decision
We will extend the current `ipfs://` URI scheme to also support IPNS names. The `ipfs://` prefix will remain, and the content of the URI will be parsed to determine if it is a hash or an IPNS name. If both are provided, the hash takes precedence.

This decision means that `ipfs://` URIs will refer to content-addressed as well as IPNS-addressed content. This allows for more flexibility, while keeping the number of different URI schemas to a minimum.

### Consequences
- `ipfs://<hash>`: This will continue to work as before, identifying a specific content hash.
- `ipfs://<ipns-name>`: This will now be a valid URI, identifying an IPNS record by its name.
- `ipfs://<hash>?name=<ipns-name>`: This will be a valid URI. The `hash` will take precedence if both are present. The `ipns-name` can be used as a fallback or for informational/caching purposes.
- Implementations of the `ipfs://` URI scheme will need to be updated to parse and handle both content hashes and IPNS names.
- This change will make the extension loading more robust by allowing for mutable references through IPNS.

## Context

Currently peers for messaging are hardcoded in the app. This means we can't
easily scale, as some of these nodes might fill up when we have more than N
active users.

Discovery v5 protocol (https://ideas.status.im/ideas/092-disc-v5-research,
https://github.com/fjl/p2p-drafts/blob/master/discv5-eip.md) allow us to
discover new peers from the app and scale server peers in our cluster
independently. This is vital for high availability/reliability and security.
decision:
## Decision 
We will use Discv5 to discover new peers. This will enable us to scale the number of peers dynamically, ensuring high availability and reliability for messaging.

### Workflow:
1.  **Node Startup:** Upon startup, each messaging node will initiate a Discv5 client.
2.  **Initial Peer Discovery:** Nodes will connect to a set of bootstrap nodes (initially hardcoded, but this can be evolved to a more dynamic mechanism in the future) to seed their discovery process.
3.  **Peer Table Maintenance:** The Discv5 client will actively maintain a Kademlia-like routing table of known peers.
4.  **Peer Discovery Requests:** When a messaging node needs to send a message and its current set of known peers is insufficient or overloaded, it will query Discv5 for suitable peers.
5.  **Peer Connectivity:** Once new peers are discovered through Discv5, the messaging node will attempt to establish connections with them to expand its network capacity.
6.  **Periodic Re-discovery:** Nodes will periodically re-query Discv5 to discover new peers and update their routing tables, ensuring the network remains robust and adapts to changes in the cluster.

### Benefits:
*   **Scalability:** Allows for the dynamic addition of new messaging nodes without requiring application code changes.
*   **High Availability:** If a messaging node goes down, Discv5 can help in discovering alternative peers, maintaining network connectivity.
*   **Reliability:** Reduces the risk of individual nodes becoming a single point of failure or bottleneck.
*   **Security:** Discv5 provides mechanisms for peer authentication and ensures that communication is with legitimate nodes.

## Context

On the path to releasing a usable beta we've faced a variety of performance
issues:

- https://github.com/status-im/ideas/issues/55
- https://ideas.status.im/ideas/071-low-traffic
- https://ideas.status.im/ideas/076-smooth-ui
- https://ideas.status.im/ideas/083-energy-efficient

Some of these performance issues are related to the use of LES, especially on
Mainnet. Examples of problems include: slow/hot sync, disk filling up, bandwidth
usage, etc. This can partly be remedied by the use of CHT to speed up sync
(https://github.com/status-im/status-go/wiki/Updating-CHT-BloomTrie).

In order to simplify the problem, we decided earlier this year to not spend too
much time looking into performance improvements related to LES, instead focusing
our efforts on improving the performance on Whisper and in client-side code.

This also means we don't have a full picture of to what extent LES is a
performance bottleneck for the Status app. It is possible proper use of CHT,
slowing sync down, vary load depending on if you are on WiFi or not, etc, can
solve these problems. However, the consensus right now is that ULC is the more
promising route to take.

However, since ULC isn't ready yet, this means we are relying on Infura. This
is a bad idea from a decentralization and security point of view. This can be
partly remedied by allowing the user to run an upstream node. It is still a bad
trust model, relying on third-party Ethereum nodes, and we want to get away
from this as soon as possible.

With ULC it is possible to connect to more than one node, which increases
decentralization and security.
decision:
## Decision 

We will transition from LES to ULC. In the meantime, we will use Infura as a backup.
This will allow us to address the current performance issues related to LES, while also improving the decentralization and security of the Status app.

This decision means that for a period of time, the Status app will rely on Infura, which is a centralized third-party service. This is a temporary measure, and we will work to transition to ULC as soon as possible.
We will also investigate ways to allow users to run an upstream node, which will further improve decentralization and security.

## Context

We have some data that we don't want to appear in the logs (user passwords are
a good example). Currently, they are passed around as strings, that could be
printed out by mistake in a log entry (see https://github.com/status-im/status-mobile/issues/4053)
decision:
## Decision
We'll create a `SecretString` type that represents sensitive data.
This type will be opaque, and will not directly expose the string data.
It will be possible to pass `SecretString`s to functions that explicitly
expect them, and which are therefore aware of their sensitive nature.
It will also be possible to explicitly convert a `SecretString` to a
regular `String`, for example, if the value needs to be used in an
API that requires a `String`. This conversion will be explicit, to ensure
that the sensitive nature of the data is not forgotten.

Here's an example:

```kotlin
// Create a sensitive string
val mySecret = SecretString("my-password")

// Pass it to a function that knows how to handle sensitive data
someSensitiveApi.authenticate(username, mySecret)

// Or explicitly convert it to a string if needed (e.g. for an API call)
val myString = mySecret.asString()
someOtherApi.doSomething(myString) // This could potentially log the string
```

**Benefits:**

* **Clearer intent:** The `SecretString` type clearly communicates that the
  data is sensitive and should be handled with care.
* **Reduced accidental logging:** By making the sensitive data opaque, it
  becomes harder to accidentally print it to logs or other output.
* **Improved security:** This approach helps reduce the risk of sensitive
  information being exposed in logs or other unintended places.
* **Explicit conversion:** The explicit `asString()` conversion forces
  developers to acknowledge and take responsibility for exposing sensitive data.

**Drawbacks:**

* **Increased boilerplate:** Introducing a new type might require some
  boilerplate code for converting between `SecretString` and `String`.
* **Adoption effort:** Existing code that handles sensitive strings will
  need to be updated to use the `SecretString` type.

**Alternatives Considered:**

* **Runtime checks and logging obfuscation:** We could implement runtime
  checks to obfuscate sensitive data before logging. However, this
  approach is more error-prone and can be bypassed if the data is
  converted to a string before the obfuscation step. It also doesn't
  prevent the sensitive data from being passed around as plain strings
  in the first place.
* **Annotation-based solutions:** Annotating sensitive fields or parameters
  could provide some guidance, but it doesn't offer the same level of
  type-safety and protection against accidental exposure as a dedicated
  `SecretString` type.

## Context

Originally, we supported 3rd party status extensions in form of javascript jailed execution environment (eq Jail) + small js library exposing chat commands API to js code.

While neat in theory, it has some serious downsides:

- Design of the API was quite poor, preferring mutable semantics over stateless API leveraging strength of the host application (cljs/re-frame).
  As a result of that, more dynamic/state requiring things (like the live tx detail in `/send` command messages) were very hard to do,
  so instead of "eating our own dogfood", we decided to side-step the API and implement such things as hard-coded logic in the app, while partly
  retaining the js code for "easier" things (like parameter declaration).
  Needles to say, such efforts produced code of very poor quality, riddling our app with hard-coded "magic" everywhere in the codebase, completely
  defeating the point of "dogfooding" while still requiring more effort and being much more error prone (no way to unit test jail logic) because 
  of the need to asynchronously communicate with jail for leftover logic in command messages (the parts not hardcoded in app).
  
- We were in a state where there was not even one command defined completely in jail, with all of them requiring custom hardcoded logic in app to
  actually work.
  Due to numerous changes and rush to get things working, half of the API was obsolete and was not working/working differently then described in
  the API documentation.
  
- We are quite tight stretched regarding performance and the Jail didn't particularly help with that - whenever some command message was defined in
  Jail, it required constant RN Bridge "ping-pong" whenever sending the message or receiving the message, eating more resources + breaking otherwise
  quite simple logic into harder to reason asynchronous call chains (execute method defined in Jail, wait for the result, execute next method in Jail...).
  
- Till now, there was no real interest in 3rd party bots anyway - the only "real" DAPPs submitted to status were "normal" DAPPs utilising just the `web3.js`
  API and built on top of regular web technologies, so they could be ran in any Ethereum client like Metamask or Mist, besides Status.
  
- There is a very promising new concept of extensions (project pluto), which will enable to extend status with much nicer and declarative extension
  definitions.
  Such extensions will not be able to only hook-in into the command messages logic, but also other application (host) hooks, like wallet assets/collectibles,
  chat contacts, etc.
decision:
## Decision 
We will remove support for all 3rd party chat command extensions using the Javascript jailed execution environment. All chat commands (including those for `send` and `dapp`) will be implemented natively within the application.

This decision is driven by the following considerations:

*   **API Quality and Maintainability:** The existing JavaScript API has proven to be inadequate for complex, stateful interactions, leading to a fragmented codebase with hard-coded logic and poor testability. Moving to native implementation allows us to leverage the strengths of the host application (ClojureScript/re-frame) and ensure consistent, high-quality code.
*   **Performance:** Eliminating the asynchronous communication overhead between the native application and the JavaScript jail will improve performance and simplify the logic for processing chat commands.
*   **Lack of Adoption:** There has been no significant adoption of third-party chat command bots, indicating that the current extension mechanism is not fulfilling a critical need.
*   **Future-Proofing:** The upcoming "Project Pluto" offers a more comprehensive and declarative approach to extensions, which will provide a superior framework for integrating external functionalities in the future. Focusing on native implementations now will allow us to transition more smoothly to Pluto's architecture without carrying legacy technical debt.

This change will simplify the codebase, improve performance, and align our development efforts with a more robust and future-proof extension strategy.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

In the light of points above, we decided to remove Jail and `Status.js` API from the application and re-work command messages in set of nicely
encapsulated app level protocols, so command related logic will be defined in one place, commands will be able to leverage strength of our platform
and development of any new functionality related to them will be much faster and more pleasant. 
We will address the 3rd party code issue separately by extensions.

## Context

The whitepaper describes Tribute to Talk (TtT) as an economics-based anti-spam filter for receiving messages and "cold" contact requests from user. Stakeholders would stake a minimum amount of SNT that another Status stakeholder must deposit in order to contact him directly.
The whitepaper also proposes that the deposit is only forfeited to the recipient if he replies.
decision:
## Decision 

The Tribute-to-Talk protocol has evolved beyond the initial idea in the whitepaper; now the deposit is transferred to the recipient whether he replies or not. The decision is made with the following points in mind:

- The initial proposal to forfeit the deposit only on reply has a fundamental flaw regarding "griefing" (the systematic harassment of a particular user): it would provide users with a mechanism to spam someone for free by simply ignoring their message.
- The intention of TtT is to make direct messaging between strangers costly; the recipient should be compensated for the value of their attention if someone wants to reach them directly.
- The purpose of TtT is not to filter messages by ensuring messages are "worth" replying to. That would be up to the recipient to decide.
- We will provide additional means for recipients to filter unwanted messages, such as blocking.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Considering:
- the absence of efficient ways to perform anonymous transactions (zk-snarks could be used in the future for that)
- the impossibility to prove that a recipient has made an actual reply and not some kind of automated reply (captcha solution was proposed, but wouldn't be practical until we can use a solution such as swarm feeds that allow users to make free updates to their captcha without on-chain transactions)
- the limited time to develop the feature

We opted for a solution that:
- doesn't establish a direct correlation between the tribute payment and an on-chain transaction, so it
- uses regular transactions for tributes payment, giving users plausible deniability about the nature of the payment
- doesn't store tribute information on-chain

## Context

During the development of a new Sylius API (based on API Platform) for Product Options, we had to decide how we should handle
Product Option's values collection, to make it efficient and easy to use.
decision:
## Decision 
We decided to store the Product Option values in a custom, dedicated entity (similar to Product Attributes). This allows us to store arbitrary values (numbers, strings, booleans, dates, etc.) and easily extend them with new types (e.g., color pickers for visual options).

This approach offers the following advantages:

- **Flexibility:** We can support various types of product option values without modifying the core `ProductOption` entity.
- **Extensibility:** Adding new product option value types (e.g., a "color" type with specific validation logic) becomes straightforward.
- **Performance:** For products with a large number of options and values, storing them separately can improve query performance.
- **API Platform Integration:** This approach aligns well with API Platform's philosophy of resource-oriented APIs, where each entity is a distinct resource. This allows for dedicated API endpoints for managing product option values, offering more granular control.

The alternative considered was embedding the values directly within the `ProductOption` entity (e.g., as a serialized array or JSONB field). This was rejected due to:

- **Lack of Type Safety:** Storing mixed types in a single field can lead to runtime errors and make data validation difficult.
- **Limited Querying Capabilities:** Querying and filtering based on specific option values would be more complex and less efficient.
- **API Platform Limitations:** API Platform works best with clearly defined entities and properties, making embedded arrays less ideal for a robust and extensible API.
- **Maintenance Complexity:** As the number of option types grows, managing and validating the embedded data would become increasingly complex.

## Context

Decisions that affect the development of Terraform Controller that are not
captured via a proposal need to be captured in some way. We need a method that
is lightweight and easy to discover the decision that have been made. The record
of decisions will help future contributors to the project to understand why
something has been implemented or is done a certain way.
decision:
## Decision 
We will use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture design decisions for Terraform Controller.

ADRs are a lightweight way to record architectural decisions, their context, and consequences. They are especially useful for distributed teams and open-source projects to maintain a shared understanding of the project's evolution.

### ADR Structure:

Each ADR will follow a consistent structure:

*   **Title:** A concise, self-explanatory name.
*   **Status:** Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Superseded (by [ADR-XXX]).
*   **Context:** Describes the forces, motivations, and problems that led to the decision.
*   **Decision:** The chosen solution or course of action.
*   **Consequences:** The positive and negative implications of the decision, including potential trade-offs.

### Workflow:

1.  **Propose:** A contributor identifies a decision that needs to be documented and creates a new ADR in a `docs/adr` directory with a "proposed" status.
2.  **Discuss:** The ADR is shared with relevant stakeholders (e.g., core contributors, maintainers) for review and discussion. This can happen through pull requests, issue trackers, or dedicated meetings.
3.  **Accept/Reject:** Once consensus is reached, the ADR's status is updated to "accepted" or "rejected." If accepted, the ADR becomes part of the project's official documentation. If rejected, it still serves as a record of why a particular approach was not chosen.
4.  **Supersede:** If an accepted decision is later reconsidered and a new decision is made, a new ADR is created, and the old ADR's status is updated to "superseded" with a link to the new ADR.

### Benefits:

*   **Transparency:** Provides a clear record of design choices.
*   **Shared Understanding:** Helps all contributors, new and old, understand the rationale behind the system's design.
*   **Historical Context:** Allows revisiting past decisions and understanding why they were made.
*   **Knowledge Transfer:** Reduces reliance on individual memory for project history.
*   **Lightweight:** Less formal and cumbersome than extensive design documents.

This approach aligns with the need for a lightweight, discoverable, and easy-to-understand method for capturing design decisions in Terraform Controller.

## Context

To detect pull request changes, we can use webhooks or polling using GitHub's
API.
decision:
## Decision
We'll use webhooks to detect pull request changes. Webhooks are generally
preferred over polling when near real-time updates are important. Using webhooks
eliminates the need to manage API rate limits, which would be a concern with
polling, and reduces the amount of unnecessary traffic. Polling also wastes
resources by making frequent requests even when no changes have occurred, whereas
webhooks are event-driven and only send data when a specific action happens.
While webhooks introduce the need for a publicly accessible endpoint and secure
verification of payloads, the benefits outweigh the additional setup and
security considerations for our use case.

## Decision

We decided to start with polling for security reasons. Using webhooks would require users to
open an ingress to the cluster. Because of this requirement, we think security conscious folks may refuse to roll this out on production clusters especially in an
air-gapped environment. This does not mean that we will never consider using webhooks for this, but that initially, polling is what we have chosen to implement.

2. Informer: Make a comment when new plan output is available.

context:
## Context

Like [Flux](https://fluxcd.io/), the tf-controller API has a handful
of places where it accepts cross-namespace references.

 - `Terraform.spec.sourceRef` -- refers to the Flux source object with
   the Terraform program
 - `Terraform.spec.dependsOn[]` -- refers to other objects that must
   be ready before this object can be run
 - `.data.resources[]` -- in the config struct used by the branch
   planner

In general in Kubernetes, references to objects in other namespaces
are frowned upon, because

 - they break namespace isolation assurances; and,
 - they encourage the proliferation of permissions.

Both of these effects make a system less secure.

However: removing cross-namespace refs entirely would break some
installations in a way that would be difficult to fix, because Flux
deployments often rely on defining sources away from objects that use
them.
decision:
## Decision
When the tf-controller API has cross-namespace references, we will add a
field `crossNamespace: true`.

Specifically:

 - `Terraform.spec.sourceRef` -- will have a `crossNamespace` field.
 - `Terraform.spec.dependsOn[]` -- will have a `crossNamespace` field.
 - `.data.resources[]` -- in the config struct used by the branch
   planner, will have a `crossNamespace` field.

This provides an explicit opt-in for users to make cross-namespace
references. This opt-in will have two effects:

1. It makes the security implications of cross-namespace references
   explicit. When users provide this field, it's clear that they're
   doing something that breaks namespace isolation.
2. It makes it easier to enforce a policy that disallows
   cross-namespace references. If a cluster operator wants to enforce
   namespace isolation, it's easy to write an admission controller or
   policy agent that disallows `crossNamespace: true`.
predicted_decision:
## Decision

Deny cross-namespace references by default, but allow them to be
enabled with a flag.

So that the default value means the right thing, the flag name must be
`enable-cross-namespace-refs`, and the default `false`. To avoid
confusion when people try to use the Flux version of this flag
`--disable-cross-namespace-refs`, it should be supported too, but only
respected if supplied.

context:
## Context

The TF-Controller currently faces challenges related to the deletion of Terraform resources.
These problems span across three categories:

1. Single object deletion,
2. Resources with dependencies deletion, and
3. Namespace deletion.

These problems must be fixed in the above order as (2) and (3) require single object deletion to be resolved first.

Deleting a single TF object can sometimes be obstructed because it's tied to other resources like Source objects, Secrets, and ConfigMaps. If we try to remove it without deleting these resources, the TF object gets stuck in an inconsistent state, making it harder for users to manage their infrastructure smoothly.
Therefore, the TF-Controller is being enhanced to address this problem more efficiently, using the contents of generated Workspace BLOBs. Each BLOB contains all necessary information from the associated Source, Secrets, and ConfigMaps to ensure that TF-Controller finalization procedures can delete objects correctly.

Currently, the TF-Controller downloads a Source BLOB and pushes it to a tf-runner. The tf-runner processes this BLOB to create a Workspace file system. It generates a backend configuration file, variable files, and other necessary files for the Workspace file system, using data from associated Secrets and ConfigMaps. This newly created Workspace file system is then compressed, sent back to the TF-Controller, and stored as a Workspace BLOB in the controller's storage.
A caching mechanism for these BLOBs is essential to fixing the single TF object deletion process.
decision:
## Decision
We propose that the TF-Controller caches the Workspace BLOBs in its local storage instead of fetching the Source BLOB every time and creating a Workspace BLOB from scratch.

This will improve the efficiency and reliability of the TF-Controller operations in the following ways:
- **Consistent Deletion**: Ensure TF objects can be consistently deleted by retaining all necessary information (from Source, Secrets, ConfigMaps) within the cached Workspace BLOB. This allows for correct finalization procedures, even if the original dependencies are no longer available.
- **Reduced External Dependencies**: Minimize reliance on external resources during deletion. By having the complete Workspace context readily available, the controller can process deletions without needing to re-fetch or re-create the workspace from potentially absent or altered Source, Secret, or ConfigMap objects.
- **Improved Performance**: Decrease the time taken for deletion operations by eliminating the need to re-download Source BLOBs, re-process them, and re-create Workspace file systems for each deletion attempt.
- **Enhanced Reliability in Edge Cases**: Address scenarios where Source, Secret, or ConfigMap objects might have been deleted prior to the TF object, preventing the TF object from getting stuck in an inconsistent state during deletion.

The cached Workspace BLOBs will contain:
- The backend configuration file.
- Variable files.
- All other necessary files derived from associated Secrets and ConfigMaps for the Workspace file system.

The caching mechanism will be implemented as follows:
1. When a Workspace BLOB is successfully generated by the `tf-runner` and returned to the TF-Controller, it will be stored in the controller's local storage.
2. For subsequent operations, particularly deletion, the TF-Controller will first attempt to retrieve the relevant Workspace BLOB from its cache.
3. If the BLOB is found in the cache, it will be used for the finalization and deletion procedures.
4. If the BLOB is not found or is invalidated (e.g., due to changes in source or dependencies, requiring a new plan/apply), a new Workspace BLOB will be generated and cached.

   * [The persistence mechanism used by the Source Controller](https://fluxcd.io/flux/installation/configuration/vertical-scaling/#persistent-storage-for-flux-internal-artifacts) will be adopted for the TF-Controller's persistence volume.
3. **BLOB Encryption**
   * The encryption and decryption of the BLOBs will be tasked to the runner, with the controller solely responsible for storing encrypted BLOBs.
   * Each namespace will require a service account, preferably named "tf-runner".
   * The token of this service account, which is natively supported by Kubernetes, will serve as the most appropriate encryption key because it's stored in a Secret, access to which can be controlled by RBAC. Storing it in a Secret also allows the key to be rotated.
4. **Security Measures (Based on STRIDE Analysis)**
   * **Spoofing:** Implement Kubernetes RBAC for access restrictions and use mutual authentication for gRPC communications.
   * **Tampering:** Use checksums for integrity verification and 0600 permissions to write-protect local disk storage.
   * **Repudiation:** Ensure strong logging and auditing mechanisms for tracking activities.
   * **Information Disclosure:** Utilize robust encryption algorithms, rotate encryption keys periodically, and secure service account tokens.
   * **Denial of Service:** Monitor storage space and automate cleanup processes.
   * **Elevation of Privilege:** Minimize permissions associated with service account tokens.
5. **First MVP & Future Planning**
   * For the initial MVP, the default pod local volume will be used.
   * Since a controller restart will erase the BLOB cache, consideration for using persistent volumes should be made for subsequent versions.

## Context

In previous releases of Zarf, the creation of the initialization package at the core of many of our E2E tests required repository secrets to login to registry1. Since this is an open-source project, anyone could submit a change to one of our GitHub workflows that could steal our secrets. In order to protect our secrets from any bad-actors we used [peter-evans/slash-command-dispatch@v2](https://github.com/peter-evans/slash-command-dispatch) so that only a maintainer would have the ability to run the E2E tests when a PR is submitted for review.

In the current version of Zarf (v0.15) images from registry1 are no longer needed to create the zarf-init-{{arch}}.tar.zst. This means, given our current span of E2E tests, we no longer need to use repository secrets when running tests. This gives us the ability to reassess the way we do our E2E testing.

When considering how to handle the tests, some of the important additions we were considering were:
  1. Ability to test against different kubernetes distributions
  2. Ability to test against different linux distributions
  3. Ability to run (at least some of) the E2E tests locally without relying on an ec2 instance - for quicker feedback loops when developing new features
decision:
## Decision 

We will transition our E2E testing to a local kind-based setup. The primary mechanism for this will be an additional GitHub Actions workflow called `e2e-suite.yml`, which will run on every PR and push to `main`. This workflow will encompass our current E2E testing as well as the new features detailed in the context.

To achieve testing against different Kubernetes distributions, we will use the `matrix` strategy in GitHub Actions to build against different versions of Kind (k8s versions) and other Kubernetes tooling (e.g., `kubectl`, `helm`). This will allow us to easily add or remove different Kubernetes versions for testing as needed.

To test against different Linux distributions, we will also use the `matrix` strategy, but this time to build and test Zarf within different Docker images representing various Linux distributions (e.g., Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS). This will ensure Zarf's compatibility across a wider range of operating environments.

For local testing and quicker feedback loops, we will create a `Makefile` target (e.g., `make e2e-local`) that developers can use to run a subset or all of the E2E tests directly on their local machines. This target will leverage the same Kind-based setup and test scripts used in the CI/CD pipeline, allowing developers to reproduce and debug issues more efficiently without relying on remote infrastructure.

The existing `slash-command-dispatch` workflow will be deprecated or removed as it is no longer necessary given the absence of repository secrets for `zarf-init` creation. This change will simplify the testing process and make it more accessible to all contributors.

## Context

In order to create any workloads in K8s, an image has to exist on the node or be pulled in from an OCI Distribution server (docker registry). Local K8s distros such as KIND, K3D, K3S, Microk8s have CLI support for injecting or pushing images into the CRIs of cluster nodes. No standard or tool exists to do this generically in K8s as the CRI sits outside the problem of K8s beyond just communicating with it. For Zarf to push images into a K8s cluster that does not have a CLI option to inject the image, we have to establish some mechanism to create a temporary registry, use an existing one, or inject the image in the cluster. Zarf must also support unknown environments with no other dependencies; we cannot assume a registry exists. Typically when K8s pulls images from a remote registry, it sends the request to the CRI that then does the pull outside of the K8s context. The CRI runs at the host level on a per-node basis, so to access a private registry, the TLS trust needs to be modified on any host/node that would attempt to pull the image. The two primary ways to do this are modifying the node's root certificate authorities or the CRIs configuration if it has an option for TLS root CA. Lastly, as this is per node, all nodes in the cluster would need to be modified or some affinity/taint to force the pod to use a single node during bootstrapping.
decision:
## Decision 
We will inject images directly into the cluster (Zarf managed registry) using a sidecar pattern to push the images into the embedded registry. Since the registry is internal and does not require TLS, there will be no need to modify the CRI (container runtime interface) of the host/node. The sidecar will be used as the initial entry point of a zarf init package or a custom package deployment to populate the internal registry and then exit. The other containers in the pod can then be run as normal after the sidecar completes its task.
### Why not use a temporary registry?
Using a temporary registry still requires TLS, or the CRI configuration for the node/host would need to be modified. This is not ideal as we want to avoid modifying the host/node directly if possible. It also requires a separate registry to be deployed, which adds complexity and overhead.
### Why not use an existing registry?
Using an existing registry would require the user to provide the registry information (URL, credentials, etc.) and ensure that the registry is accessible from the cluster. This adds complexity for the user and requires external dependencies, which Zarf aims to avoid.
### Why use a sidecar?
A sidecar pattern allows us to leverage the existing Kubernetes infrastructure to deploy a container that can push images into the internal registry. This avoids the need for external tools or dependencies and simplifies the process of injecting images into the cluster. The sidecar can be part of the initial `zarf init` package, ensuring that the internal registry is populated before any other applications are deployed. It also provides a clean way to manage the lifecycle of the image injection process.

## Decision

Because we cannot require third-party dependencies, the requirement from some cloud-managed or distro-managed registry is not an option as not every K8s cluster will have that available.  Running an in-memory registry while zarf is performing `zarf init` was initially explored to resolve the external dependency issue.  However, this solution proved too complex when dealing with network traversal (especially behind NATs), firewall, and NACL rulesets.  Additionally, because of the complexities around TLS trust, the in-memory registry was not a viable solution.

After iterating on several solutions, including `kubectl cp`, `kubectl exec`, a busybox configmap injection that brought in netcat to stream files, and a few variations on those ideas, we found using only configmaps to be the most predictable method for injection. The challenge with this mode is that the ETCD limit is 1 MB total, with binary data base64-encoded leaving roughly 670 KBs of data per configmap, far too small to bring the registry tarball in a single configmap. So instead, we used a combination of a custom Rust binary compiled with MUSL to perform file concatenation, untarring, and verification of a set of split tarball chunks across a variable number of configmaps. We found that chunking by less than the near-maximum configmap size was more performant on some resource-constrained control planes. The details of this solution and a drawing are located in the main README of this repo.

## Context

Currently Zarf leverages [Helm Post Rendering](https://helm.sh/docs/topics/advanced/#post-rendering) to mutate image paths and secrets for K8s to use the internal [Zarf Registry](../packages/zarf-registry/). This works well for simple K8s deployments where Zarf is performing the actual manifest apply but fails when using a secondary gitops tools suchs as [Flux](https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2), [ArgoCD](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), etc. At that point, Zarf is unable to provide mutation and it is dependent on the package author to do the mutations themselves using rudimentary templating. Further, this issue also exists when for CRDs that references the [git server](../packages/gitea/). A `zarf prepare` command was added previously to make this less painful, but it still requires additional burden on package authors to do something we are able to prescribe in code.
decision:
## Decision 
We will implement an OCI-standard image content trust and signing feature to address the current limitations of Zarf's image mutation and secret handling, especially when used with GitOps tools like Flux or ArgoCD. This feature will focus on securely transforming image references and other sensitive data within Kubernetes manifests *before* they are applied or committed to a Git repository for GitOps consumption.

Here's how it will work:

1.  **Image Transformation Phase:**
    *   **Pre-Signing Transformation:** When a Zarf package is being created or prepared, a dedicated phase will identify and transform all external image references within Kubernetes manifests to point to the internal Zarf registry. This transformation will leverage a more robust parsing and rewriting mechanism than simple string replacement, potentially using a dedicated tool or library that understands Kubernetes manifest structures.
    *   **CRD/Git Server Reference Transformation:** Similar to images, references to the Zarf Git server within CRDs or other manifests will also be identified and rewritten to point to the internal Zarf Git server.
    *   **Secret Injection/Templating:** Instead of direct mutation, Zarf will support a more secure and flexible mechanism for handling secrets. This could involve:
        *   **Dynamic Secret Generation:** Allowing package authors to define secret templates that Zarf can populate with environment-specific values during deployment.
        *   **Sealed Secrets Integration:** Providing built-in support for tools like Sealed Secrets, where secrets are encrypted at rest and decrypted by a controller in the cluster.
    *   **Manifest Rewriting:** The output of this phase will be a set of rewritten Kubernetes manifests where all internal references (images, Git servers) are updated, and secrets are handled securely.

2.  **Content Trust and Signing:**
    *   **Manifest Signing:** After the transformation phase, the rewritten Kubernetes manifests (including any generated secrets or secret references) will be cryptographically signed using OCI-standard signing mechanisms (e.g., Notary v2, Cosign). This signature will attest to the integrity and origin of the manifests.
    *   **Signature Verification:** During deployment (either directly by Zarf or by a GitOps tool), the signatures on the manifests will be verified against a trusted public key. This ensures that the manifests have not been tampered with since they were signed by Zarf.
    *   **SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) Integration:** The signing process will also generate or incorporate an SBOM for the package, detailing all components, dependencies, and their versions. This enhances transparency and auditability.

3.  **GitOps Compatibility:**
    *   **Signed Manifests in Git:** The signed and transformed manifests will be committed to a Git repository. GitOps tools like Flux or ArgoCD will then pull these manifests from Git.
    *   **In-Cluster Verification:** GitOps controllers will be configured to verify the OCI signatures on the manifests before applying them to the cluster. This moves the verification step closer to the application point and leverages the built-in security features of the GitOps tool.
    *   **Pre-Deployment Hooks:** Zarf will provide pre-deployment hooks that GitOps tools can invoke to perform any final environment-specific adjustments or secret injections, if necessary, while still maintaining the integrity provided by the signing.

**Benefits:**

*   **Enhanced Security:** Cryptographic signing ensures the integrity and authenticity of manifests, preventing tampering.
*   **Seamless GitOps Integration:** GitOps tools can consume Zarf packages directly from Git with confidence, as image and Git server references are already transformed and manifests are signed.
*   **Reduced Package Author Burden:** Package authors no longer need to manually template image paths or Git server references. Zarf handles these transformations automatically.
*   **Improved Auditability:** Signed manifests and SBOMs provide a clear audit trail of what was deployed.
*   **Standard Compliance:** Leveraging OCI standards for content trust and signing aligns Zarf with broader industry practices.
*   **Flexibility for Secrets:** A more robust secret handling mechanism provides greater flexibility and security for sensitive data.

## Context

In ADR 3, the decision was made to create a rust binary (`stage1`) that would re-assemble a `registry:2` image and a go registry binary (`stage2`) from a series of configmaps. While this solution works, it is overkill for the operations that `stage2` performs. The `stage2` binary is only responsible for 1. starting a docker registry in `rw` mode, 2. pushing the `registry:2` crane tarball into said registry, 3. starting the docker registry in `r` mode. This `registry:2` image is then immediately consumed by the `zarf-registry` package, creating a true in-cluster docker registry. The injector pod is then destroyed. The overhead this operation creates:

- having to keep track of another binary (making the total number 3 for the zarf ecosystem)
- nearly doubling the amount of configmaps loaded into the cluster (makes init slower)
- having to compile the binary for each platform (adds to the build time + ci)
- using a full-featured docker registry to host a single image (wasteful)
decision:
## Decision 
The `stage2` go binary and its associated configmaps will be removed. In its place, the `stage1` rust binary will:

1. Create a `tmpfs` volume in the pod to act as the registry.
2. Re-assemble the `registry:2` tarball into the `tmpfs` volume.
3. Start a small, custom http server in the same rust binary.
4. Serve the tarball from the `tmpfs` volume over http.
5. `zarf-init` will then pull the tarball directly from this ephemeral server and push it into the zarf-registry.
6. `zarf-init` will delete the pod when the operation is complete.

This will reduce:
- the number of binaries that need to be maintained from 3 to 2
- the number of configmaps loaded into the cluster by ~50%
- the overall build time by reducing the number of binaries needing to be built/tested across multiple platforms
- the resource overhead by removing the full-fledged docker registry in favor of a simpler http server

context:
## Context

There are sections of the code that are not easily able to be tested by our end-to-end testing and now that Zarf is moving into being a library for other products there will be more scrutiny around our defined interfaces.  This ADR explores ways that we could adjust our testing strategy to address these concerns.

Potential considerations:

1. Introduce Unit-Testing Zarf-wide
    Pros:
        - More of the codebase is covered with tests and will force us to take more consideration when updating it
    Cons:
        - As the codebase evolves the efficacy of these tests is likely to go down, especially if they are written to the code rather than the interface

2. Introduce Unit Testing in a defined and limited capacity within Zarf
    Pros:
        - A decent amount of the codebase will be tested (specifically we can target those areas difficult to e2e test)
        - We can be picky about what/where we unit test so that the maintenance burden of the tests is not too high
    Cons:
        - We will need to be vigilant when PRs come through with Unit Tests that these are correct applications of them

3. Introduce Integration Testing or partial End-to-End testing
    Pros:
        - This is closer to how we already test within Zarf
    Cons:
        - These can be relatively complex to orchestrate and maintain over time requiring complex mocks or other mechanisms to make them work
decision:
## Decision

We will introduce unit testing into Zarf in a defined and limited capacity, focusing on areas of the codebase that are difficult to test with end-to-end (e2e) tests and on our publicly exposed interfaces. This approach balances the need for increased test coverage and interface scrutiny with the practical considerations of test maintenance and development velocity.

**Key Principles for Unit Testing in Zarf:**

*   **Targeted Application:** Unit tests will primarily focus on:
    *   **Public Interfaces:** To ensure the stability and correctness of Zarf when used as a library by other products. This includes functions, structs, and methods intended for external consumption.
    *   **Complex Logic/Edge Cases:** Sections of the code with intricate business logic, complex algorithms, or extensive error handling that are difficult to fully exercise through higher-level tests.
    *   **Components Difficult to E2E Test:** Areas that require significant setup, external dependencies, or specific environmental conditions that make e2e testing impractical or overly burdensome.
*   **Interface-Driven, Not Implementation-Driven:** Unit tests should primarily validate the *behavior* and *contract* of a unit (function, method, class) rather than its internal implementation details. This makes the tests more resilient to refactoring.
*   **Isolation:** Unit tests should be isolated from external dependencies (e.g., file system, network, database, other Zarf components) through the use of mocks, stubs, or fakes. This ensures that a unit test fails only if the unit under test is faulty, not because of issues in its dependencies.
*   **Clear Ownership:** Teams or individuals responsible for a specific module or feature will also be responsible for maintaining its unit tests.
*   **Review Process:** PRs introducing new unit tests or modifying existing ones will undergo scrutiny to ensure they adhere to these principles and provide genuine value without adding undue maintenance burden. Reviewers will specifically check if the tests are:
    *   Targeted appropriately.
    *   Testing the interface/behavior rather than internal implementation.
    *   Adequately isolated.

**Rationale:**

*   **Addressing E2E Gaps:** This approach directly addresses the problem of sections of the code not being easily testable by e2e tests, thereby increasing overall code confidence.
*   **Library Readiness:** By focusing on public interfaces, we ensure that Zarf's use as a library is robust and predictable for consuming projects, which is critical for its evolving role.
*   **Maintainability:** By being selective about where unit tests are applied, we avoid the overhead of a blanket unit testing mandate, which could lead to a large suite of brittle tests. This allows us to prioritize testing effort where it yields the most benefit.
*   **Developer Empowerment:** Developers are empowered to identify and unit test critical components, fostering a sense of ownership over code quality.
*   **Controlled Introduction:** This incremental introduction allows the team to adapt to and refine the unit testing practice over time, learning what works best for the Zarf codebase without a massive upfront investment or disruption.

**Future Considerations:**

While not part of this immediate decision, the team will continue to evaluate the benefits of integration or partial e2e testing in the future, especially for scenarios where complex interactions between Zarf components (without external dependencies) are critical and unit tests alone may not suffice.

## Context

Images are not the only way that dependencies can be brought in via a Zarf package (our own init package has two components that are not images yet could have vulnerabilities within them, k3s and the injector).  We should SBOM these in addition to images so that we are providing a more complete picture to our users.

Potential considerations:

1. Run Syft against the entire zarf temp build directory
    Pros:
        - This would provide the most information for what _might_ be in a Zarf package
    Cons:
        - If git repos are brought in you could catch many index files that are actually not in the package but are dependencies of the repos leading to confusion

2. Run Syft against files and dataInjections
    Pros:
        - We know these files are actually inside of the package and won't just be noise
        - This is the most common two ways for people to include additional artifacts in packages (we use files in our own init package)
    Cons:
        - This is only a subset of what Zarf provides and someone could commit an artifact to a git repo for example

3. Allow user flexibility in what gets SBOMed
    Pros:
        - This provides the user the most flexibility
    Cons:
        - This could be complex to get right on implementation and if it were optional may be a forgotten feature by most users
decision:
## Decision 
We will run Syft against files, dataInjections, and git repos that are brought into a Zarf package to generate additional SBOMs.

1. **Files**: This will ensure that any arbitrary files included in the package (e.g., binaries, libraries, configuration files) are scanned for vulnerabilities. This is a direct and explicit inclusion method.
2. **Data Injections**: Similar to files, dataInjections are explicitly included content that directly contributes to the package's functionality and therefore should be part of the SBOM.
3. **Git Repos**: While this has the potential for some noise, the risk of missing critical dependencies embedded within a git repository's structure (especially those not explicitly listed as files or dataInjections) outweighs the con of potential index files. We will implement smart filtering or heuristics if excessive noise becomes a practical issue. The goal is to capture active dependencies within the context of the repository's intended use in the package.

This approach balances comprehensiveness with practicality. It focuses on the most common and direct ways users bring external artifacts into a Zarf package, providing a significantly more complete picture of dependencies beyond just images, while acknowledging and planning for mitigation of potential noise from git repositories.

## Context

Zarf was rooted in the idea of declarative K8s deployments for disconnected environments. Many of the design decisions made in Zarf are based on this idea. However, in certain connected environments, Zarf can still be leveraged as a way to define declarative deployments and upgrades without the constraints of disconnected environments. To that end, providing a declarative way to deploy Zarf packages without the need for a Zarf init package would be useful in such environments.
decision:
## Decision 
Zarf will adopt a "batteries included but removable" model for the `zarf init` package. Specifically, all components (git servers, artifact registries, K3s, etc) included in the init package will remain components, and each will be able to be disabled and/or configured via the `zarf init` command or `zarf.yaml`. This will allow Zarf to be used in connected environments where these components may already exist or are not desired, without the need for a separate init package. This will also allow Zarf to be used in disconnected environments where these components are desired, but with the ability to configure them to suit the needs of the environment.

context:
## Context

Originally, the `scripts` noun was added to components to allow us to move hard-coded init business logic out of the codebase and into the package system. At the time there was only a `before` and `after` section with simply an array entry per command. Later, `prepare` was added as a way to do something during `zarf package create`. As teams began to find new ways to use the capabilities, their limitations became more obvious.
decision:
## Decision
We've decided to refine the scripts noun and its behavior to allow for more flexibility and control. The changes will include:

1.  **Lifecycle Hooks:** Instead of just `before` and `after`, we will introduce a more comprehensive set of lifecycle hooks to better align with common software deployment and execution phases. These will likely include, but not be limited to: `create`, `prepare`, `deploy-before`, `deploy-after`, `start`, `stop`, `cleanup`.

2.  **Command Execution Environment:** Scripts will no longer be simple arrays of commands. Each script entry will become an object that allows for specifying:
    *   `command`: The actual command to execute.
    *   `shell`: (Optional) The shell to use for execution (e.g., `bash`, `sh`, `powershell`). If not specified, a default shell will be used.
    *   `workingDirectory`: (Optional) The directory from which to execute the command.
    *   `environment`: (Optional) A map of environment variables to set for the script's execution.
    *   `timeout`: (Optional) A duration after which the script will be terminated if not completed.
    *   `onError`: (Optional) Defines behavior if the script fails (e.g., `continue`, `fail-component`, `fail-package`).

## Context

There has been a long-standing usability gap with Zarf when doing local development due to a lack of local image support. A solution was merged in, [#1173](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/pull/1173), and released in [v0.23.4](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/releases/tag/v0.23.4) to support this feature. Unfortunately, we didn't realize there is a [glaring issue](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/issues/1214) with the implementation that causes Zarf to crash when trying to load large images into the local docker daemon.  The docker daemon support in Crane is somewhat naive and can send a machine into an OOM condition due to how the tar stream is loaded into memory from the docker save action. Crane does have an option to avoid this issue, but at the cost of being much slower to load images from docker.

We did extensive investigation into various strategies of loading docker images from the daemon including: crane, skopeo, the docker go client and executing the docker cli directly with varying levels of success. Unfortunately, some of the methods that did work well were up to 3 times slower than the current implementation, though they avoided the OOM issue. Lastly, the docker daemon save operations directly still ended up being slower than crane and docker produced a legacy format that would cause issues with [future package schema changes](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/zarf/issues/1319) we are planning for oci imports.

|                                                    | **Docker** | **Crane** |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | --------- |
| Big Bang Core (cached)                             | 3m 1s      | 1m 58s    |
| Big Bang Core (cached + skip-sbom)                 | 1m 51s     | 56s       |
| 20 GB Single-Layer Image (local registry)          |            | 6m 14s    |
| 20 GB Single-Layer Image (local registry + cached) | 5m 2s      | 2m 10s    |

## Decision 
Zarf will provide a Helm Chart to simplify the deployment of Big Bang.

### The Big Bang Zarf Package Helm Chart

The Zarf Big Bang package will contain a Helm Chart that will perform the following actions for the Zarf Agent running inside of the cluster it is deployed into:

1. Extract a `values.yaml` file from the Zarf package and use it to determine the specific set of Big Bang components that are desired.
2. Generate a `helm-values.yaml` file that will contain the values that will be used to deploy Big Bang.
3. Generate a `zarf-images.txt` file that will contain the list of images that are needed for the specific Big Bang components that are desired.
4. Generate a `zarf-repos.txt` file that will contain the list of git repositories that are needed for the specific Big Bang components that are desired.
5. Create a `zarf.yaml` file that will contain the `images` and `git` sections that are needed for the specific Big Bang components that are desired.
6. Create a Zarf package with the `zarf.yaml` file that will contain the `images` and `git` sections that are needed for the specific Big Bang components that are desired.
7. Deploy Flux into the cluster.
8. Deploy Big Bang into the cluster using the generated `helm-values.yaml` file.

### Limitations

The Zarf Big Bang package will have the following limitations:

- The Zarf Big Bang package will not be able to deploy Big Bang with all of its components due to the size of the images and git repositories that would be needed.
- The Zarf Big Bang package will not be able to deploy Big Bang with custom images or git repositories.
- The Zarf Big Bang package will not be able to deploy Big Bang with custom Flux configurations.

### Future Considerations

- Investigate a method of dynamically including images and git repositories into a Zarf package based on the values provided to the Big Bang chart.
- Investigate a method of dynamically including custom images and git repositories into a Zarf package.
- Investigate a method of dynamically including custom Flux configurations into a Zarf package.

Zarf packages are currently only available if built locally or through manual file transfers. This is not a scalable way to distribute packages. We wanted to find a way to distribute and publish packages in a way that is easily consumable for the majority of users. When considering the goal of being able to share packages, security and trust are very important considerations. We wanted our publishing solution and architecture changes to keep in mind signing of packages and the ability to verify the integrity of packages.

We know we are successful when:

1. (Priority) Users can use Zarf to natively publish a Zarf package to an OCI compliant registry
